subsection.title: Graphing Equations

assemblage.title: Linear Equation
assemblage.p: An equation of the form ~\blert{y=ax+b}~, where a and b are constants, is called a linear equation because its graph is a straight line.

subsection.p: We can graph a linear equation by evaluating the expression ax+b at several values of x and then plotting points.

statement.p:
At 6 am the temperature was 50 \degree, and it has been rising by 4 \degree every hour.
Write an equation for the temperature, T, after h hours.
Graph your equation.

ol.li: We set h=0 at 6 am. At that time, T=50. Because the temperature is rising by 4 \degree every hour, we multiply the number of hours by 4 and add the result to 50 to get the new temperature. Thus, our equation is T=50+4h.

li.p: Step 1: We make a table of values for the equation. We choose some values for h, as shown in the first column of the table below. For each value of h, we evaluate the formula for T, and we record these values in the second column of the table.

Step 2: We use the values in the table to help us choose scales for the axes. For this graph, the input values are less than 10, but the largest output value is 70. We use increments of 1 on the horizontal or h-axis and increments of 10 on the vertical or T-axis.
Step 3: Each ordered pair gives us a point on the graph. We plot the points on the grid and connect them with a smooth curve. All the points should lie on a straight line.

subsection.title: Cartesian Coordinate System
subsection.p: Many graphs include negative values as well as positive values. To make such a graph, we construct a Cartesian coordinate systemCartesian coordinate system, named after the French mathematician and philosopher René Descartes.

sidebyside.p: We draw two perpendicular number lines for the horizontal and vertical axes. The two axes divide the plane into four quadrantsquadrant, or regions, as shown at right. We often use x for the input variable inputvariable and y for the output variableoutputvariable, so the horizontal axis axishorizontal is called the x-axisx-axis and the vertical axis axisvertical is the y-axisy-axis. The axes intersect at the zero point of each number line. The coordinates of this intersection point, called the originorigin, are (0,0).

statement.p: What are the coordinates of the origin?
True or False: The x-coordinate of any point on the y-axis is zero.

The figure below shows how to plot points on a Cartesian grid. Points in the upper right quadrant have both coordinates positive. Points with negative x-coordinates are plotted to the left of the x-axis, and points with negative y-coordinates are plotted below the y-axis.
For example, the point (-2,1) is plotted 2 units to the left of the x-axis and 1 unit above the y-axis. In which quadrant are both coordinates negative?
True or False: The notation (5,3) represents two points, one on the x-axis and one on the y-axis.
True or False: If both coordinates of a point are negative, the point is located in the lower left quadrant.

assemblage.title: Graphing Tip #1
assemblage.p: If the coefficient of x (the number multiplying x) is a fraction, we can make our work easier by choosing multiples of the denominator for the x-values. That way we won't have to work with fractions to find the y-values. In the Example below, the coefficient of x is \dfrac{-2}{3}, so we choose multiples of 3 for the x-values.

ol.li: Use the graph to solve the equation ~\dfrac{-2}{3}x-4=-2

li.p: We choose x-values that are multiples of 3 and make a table of values.
Then we plot the points and connect them with a straight line.
We see that y has been replaced by -2 in the equation of the graph. So we look for the point on the graph that has y-coordinate -2. This point, labeled P on the graph below, has x-coordinate -3.

Because it lies on the graph, the point P(-3,-2) is a solution of the equation ~y=\dfrac{-2}{3}x-4. To check our solution algebraically, we substitute x=\blert{-3} and y=\alert{-2} into the equation, we get a true statement: \alert{-2}=\dfrac{-2}{3}(\blert{-3})-4 This statement also tells us that -3 is a solution of the equation ~\dfrac{-2}{3}x-4=-2.

assemblage.title: Graphing Tip #2
assemblage.p: When you graph a linear equation, you should extend the line far enough in both directions so that it will cross both the x-axis and the y-axis. The points where the graph crosses the axes are important for applications.

assemblage.title: Look Closer
assemblage.p: The graph of an equation is a picture of the solutions of the equation. Each point on the graph represents a solution. If a point lies on the graph, its coordinates make the equation true.
